title: Osimertinib with or without savolitinib as first-line treatment for MET-aberrant, EGFR-mutant NSCLC: randomized phase 2 trial (FLOWERS)
author: Anna Li; Wei-Neng Feng; Juan Li; Bing-Fei Xu; Jun Zhao; Yun Jia; Ke-Jing Tang; Yong-Sheng Li; Cheng-Zhi Zhou; Yun Fan; Chong-Rui Xu; Yue-Li Sun; Hua-Jun Chen; Hong-Hong Yan; Zong-Kun Shi; Jin-Ji Yang
text:
Abstract
To investigate the efficacy and safety of osimertinib plus savolitinib for patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations and de novo MET aberrations, we conducted a randomized, multicenter, open-label, phase 2 study (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05163249). Treatment-naïve patients with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC harboring de novo MET amplification or overexpression and EGFR mutations were randomized to receive osimertinib monotherapy (cohort 1, 80 mg orally once daily) or combination therapy (cohort 2, osimertinib 80 mg orally once daily and savolitinib 300 mg orally twice daily). The primary endpoint was the confirmed objective response rate (ORR). A total of 44 patients were randomized to either cohort 1 (n = 23) or cohort 2 (n = 21). The pre-specified study endpoint was achieved. The confirmed ORR was 60.9% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 38.5–80.3) in cohort 1 and 90.5% (95% CI: 69.6–98.8) in cohort 2, with disease control rates of 87% (95% CI: 66.4–97.2) and 95.2% (95% CI: 76.2–99.9). Treatment-related adverse events of grade 3 or higher occurred in 2 patients (8.7%) in cohort 1 and 12 patients (57.1%) in cohort 2. Osimertinib plus savolitinib showed promising antitumor activity and manageable safety.
Subject terms: Non-small-cell lung cancer, Targeted therapies, Cancer therapy
The presence of EGFR mutations and de novo MET aberrations limited response to EGFR inhibitors in patients with advance non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Here, the authors report a phase 2 randomised clinical trial investigating first-line osimertinib (EGFR inhibitor) plus savolitinib (c-MET inhibitor) in patients with MET-aberrant, EGFR-mutant advanced NSCLC.
Introduction
The prognosis of patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains poor, with 5-year overall survival (OS) rates ranging from 12 to 24%1,2. Although successive generations of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have achieved substantial improvements in efficacy and survival, approximately 20% of patients with EGFR-sensitive mutations receive limited benefit from standard EGFR TKI therapy, with marked inter-patient variability in the duration of clinical response3–5. Evidence suggests that coexisting driver mutations may underlie this variability4. Among these, MET6,7 aberrations are significant co-alterations in EGFR-mutant NSCLC4, with de novo MET amplification and MET overexpression in approximately 2–5% and 11–15% of treatment-naïve EGFR-mutant patients8–11, respectively. Mi12 et al. reported a relatively low prevalence of MET overexpression (2.5%) in a Chinese population.
De novo MET aberrations, including amplification and overexpression, may be associated with primary resistance to EGFR TKIs13. In EGFR-mutant advanced NSCLC, de novo MET aberrations have been associated with poor responses to first-line EGFR-TKI monotherapy. A subgroup analysis from the BENEFIT trial revealed significant differences in median progression-free survival (PFS) and OS between patients with EGFR mutations only and those with mutations in EGFR and oncogenes, such as MET amplification (5 of 24). When treated with first-line gefitinib, the median PFS was 13.2 months versus 4.7 months (hazard ratio: 2.66, 95% CI: 1.58–4.49, p = 0.0003), and the median OS was 32.0 months versus 21.7 months8,14. Similarly, Lai et al. 10 reported that patients with MET amplification (5 [3.2%] of 154) exhibited the shortest time to treatment failure (TTF) to EGFR TKI, with a median TTF of 5 months (range: 1.0–6.4 months). In addition, Yu et al. 11 found that patients with MET amplification (4 [2.0%]) had a median progression time of 5 months compared to 11 months in those without amplification (hazard ratio: 3.7, p = 0.019). Notably, patients with coexisting MET amplification undergoing first-line osimertinib treatment experience significantly shorter PFS and OS than those without MET amplification15. Further analysis of the cumulative TTF of EGFR TKI therapy revealed a strong trend suggesting that high MET expression was correlated with a shorter TTF16. A phase 2 study17 compared erlotinib with and without emibetuzumab (a MET monoclonal antibody) as a first-line treatment for patients with EGFR-mutant metastatic NSCLC. The results indicated that patients with EGFR mutation and high MET expression might derive a clinically meaningful difference in PFS and OS from emibetuzumab plus erlotinib.
FLAURA218 and MARIPOSA19,20 studies demonstrated that combination therapy significantly prolonged PFS compared to osimertinib monotherapy. Although first-line combination therapies have demonstrated promising results, several questions remain unanswered in clinical practice. These include a high incidence of grade 3 or higher adverse events (AEs), challenges related to drug convenience, and a lack of publicly available efficacy data on combination therapy in advanced EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients with coexisting de novo MET amplification and/or overexpression. Given the activation of EGFR and MET pathways in patients with concurrent EGFR mutations and MET amplification/overexpression, the efficacy of treatment may be further optimized by the selective administration of dual-target therapy as a first-line approach for this population. Preclinical studies have revealed that combining osimertinib with savolitinib enhances antitumor efficacy compared to monotherapy in lung cancer organoid models with EGFR mutations and MET amplification and/or overexpression21,22. Furthermore, a case series indicated that combining osimertinib with savolitinib as a first-line treatment demonstrated rapid and durable antitumor activity in previously untreated patients with advanced NSCLC with EGFR mutations and MET amplification23. MET amplification or overexpression is a mechanism of resistance to osimertinib, providing a rationale for evaluating the combination of osimertinib with savolitinib as a first-line treatment to potentially reduce MET-driven resistance. Prospective study on the efficacy of osimertinib monotherapy or osimertinib plus savolitinib in advanced NSCLC patients with coexisting EGFR mutations and de novo MET amplification and/or overexpression was limited.
In this work, we aim to evaluate the efficacy and safety of osimertinib with or without savolitinib as first-line treatment in de novo MET amplification and/or overexpression and EGFR-mutant advanced NSCLC. Osimertinib plus savolitinib shows promising antitumor activity and a manageable safety profile in treatment-naïve advanced NSCLC patients with EGFR mutations and de novo MET aberrations.
Results
Patients and treatment
Patients with MET amplification and/or overexpression who met the definition of study requirement identified by prospective tumor tissue testing (fluorescence in situ hybridization [FISH], next-generation sequencing [NGS], or immunohistochemistry [IHC]) were referred to participate in this study between May 31, 2022, and February 5, 2024. A total of 45 patients with de novo MET amplification and/or overexpression and EGFR-mutant advanced NSCLC were screened for inclusion, and 44 were randomized across 10 research centers, and assigned to either osimertinib monotherapy (cohort 1, 23 patients) or osimertinib plus savolitinib combination therapy (cohort 2, 21 patients) (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Fig. 1). All patients received at least one dose of treatment and were included in the efficacy and safety analyses.
The median age of the patients was 58 years (range: 29–74 years), with 52.3% male. Most patients (42 out of 44, 95.5%) had adenocarcinoma. 13 patients (29.6%) had brain metastasis. In total, 20 patients (45.5%) had an exon 19 deletion, and 19 (43.2%) had the L858R mutation. In addition, 36 patients (81.8%) had MET overexpression, 6 patients (13.6%) had MET amplification, and 2 patients (4.5%) had both MET amplification and overexpression. Baseline demographics and clinical characteristics are summarized in Table 1. The detailed results of MET alteration are presented in Supplementary Table 2. Baseline plasma circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) mutation analysis was conducted. The top three co-mutations identified by ctDNA analysis in all patients included the following: TP53 (72.7%), PIK3CA (13.6%), and RB1 (13.6%). The baseline ctDNA variants, including EGFR mutations and MET amplification, as well as the common co-mutations, were found to be similar between the two cohorts (Supplementary Fig. 2).

As of the data cutoff date on 28 May 2024, 15 patients (65.2%) in cohort 1 and 15 patients (71.4%) in cohort 2 continued to receive treatment. Two patients in cohort 1 who had disease progression with confirmed MET amplification and/or overexpression were crossed over to cohort 2 (Fig. 1). The median follow-up was 7.8 months (range: 2.8–23.8) in cohort 1 and 8.5 months (range: 3.7–18.7) in cohort 2.
Efficacy
In accordance with the study protocol, the analyses were descriptive only, and no statistical hypothesis testing was undertaken. The confirmed objective response rate (ORR) was 60.9% (95% CI: 38.5–80.3) in cohort 1 and 90.5% (95% CI: 69.6–98.8) in cohort 2 (Table 2 and Fig. 2a). Subgroup analysis indicated that the ORRs across multiple subgroups were consistent with those of overall patients in each cohort (Supplementary Fig. 3). In cohort 1, the best median tumor reduction rate was –42.2% (Fig. 2b). Two patients in cohort 1 with initial progressive disease transitioned to combination therapy after 4 weeks, achieving PR and remaining on combination treatment. In cohort 2, the best median tumor reduction rate was—47.7% (Fig. 2c). The disease control rate (DCR) was 87.0% (95% CI: 66.4–97.2) in cohort 1 and 95.2% (95% CI: 76.2–99.9) in cohort 2. The median duration of response (DoR) was 8.4 months (range: 6.6-NE) in cohort 1 and 18.6 months (95% CI: NR-NE) in cohort 2 (Fig. 2a).

At the time of data cutoff, the investigator-assessed median PFS was 9.3 months (95% CI: 7.4-NE) in cohort 1 and 19.6 months (95% CI: 10.2-NR) in cohort 2, with maturity of 34.8% and 23.8%, respectively (Fig. 3). At 6 months, the PFS rates were 82.1% (95% CI: 66.2–98.0) for cohort 1 and 87.3% (95% CI: 70.2–98.9) for cohort 2. The median OS was not reached, and the data are immature; the results are expected to be released at the final analysis.
Safety
All treated patients experienced at least one treatment-related AEs (TRAEs) (Table 3). The most common TRAEs in cohort 1 included diarrhea (56.5%), rash (52.2%), and pruritus (43.5%), whereas cohort 2 reported rash (52.4%), platelet count decreased (52.4%), diarrhea (42.9%), white blood cell count decreased (42.9%), alanine aminotransferase increase (42.9%), paronychia (42.9%), and peripheral edema (42.9%) (Supplementary Fig. 5, Supplementary Tables 4 and 5). Grade 3 or higher TRAEs were reported in 2 patients (8.7%) in cohort 1 compared to 12 patients (57.1%) in cohort 2 (Supplementary Table 3). Serious TRAEs were reported in 1 patient (4.3%) in cohort 1 and in 4 patients (19.0%) in cohort 2. No fatal TRAEs were recorded in either of the cohorts. In cohort 2, one patient (4.8%) experienced grade 2 interstitial lung disease, leading to permanent discontinuation of both osimertinib and savolitinib; five patients (23.8%) had permanent discontinuation of osimertinib and/or savolitinib (Table 3).

Discussion
The FLOWERS study is a randomized, multicenter, phase 2 study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of osimertinib plus savolitinib and osimertinib monotherapy in treatment-naïve, locally advanced, or metastatic NSCLC patients with EGFR mutations and de novo MET amplification and/or overexpression. The study showed a promising confirmed ORR in a combination therapy cohort. These findings suggest that EGFR mutations may not be the only dominant driver genes in this population. The insights offered by these findings may help guide personalized treatment strategies for NSCLC patients with EGFR mutations and co-mutations and suggest a potential paradigm for future clinical trials targeting dual-gene mutations.
Several clinical trials have previously been conducted to investigate the efficacy of combining MET TKIs (such as tepotinib, savolitinib, and capmatinib) with EGFR TKIs (such as gefitinib and osimertinib) in patients with EGFR-mutant, MET-amplified advanced NSCLC who have developed acquired resistance to EGFR TKI therapy. The findings indicated an ORR of approximately 50%18,24,25. Consequently, dual-target therapy as a first-line treatment may represent a viable approach to delay the onset of resistance in treatment-naïve patients with advanced EGFR-mutant NSCLC with de novo MET amplification and/or overexpression. The preliminary efficacy of first-line dual-target inhibition therapy was suggested in a phase 2 study26 involving erlotinib with a MET monoclonal antibody and case series17. However, these studies remain exploratory and are limited in scope. Therefore, the FLOWERS trial, a phase 2 study, was designed to investigate the feasibility and potential efficacy of the dual-target regimen in first-line settings. Additionally, oral dual-targeted therapy provides psychological benefits, improves daily life convenience, and reduces the utilization of hospital and ambulatory care resources. Employing a precise dual-target strategy in a highly selected patient cohort highlights the potential of precision medicine for treating patients with NSCLC with concurrent EGFR mutations and MET aberrations. Notably, one patient in the osimertinib monotherapy cohort (ECOG PS 1, stage IVB adenocarcinoma, cT4N3M1c, with extensive metastases; biomarkers: MET IHC 3+ [95%], PD-L1 [80%], EGFR exon 19 deletion [+], MET CN by NGS [3.4]) experienced disease progression within the first four weeks, which was subsequently confirmed as MET overexpression (100% 3+). Following the study protocol, this patient transitioned to combination therapy and achieved PR (Supplementary Fig. 4). The patient discontinued study treatment after 3 months due to a threefold elevation in grade 3 ALT, but on subsequent self-administered dual-targeted therapy, achieved a PFS2 of 11.4 months. Another patient in the osimertinib monotherapy cohort (ECOG PS 1, stage IVA adenocarcinoma, cT1cN2M1a, with pleural metastasis; biomarkers: MET IHC 3+ [95%], EGFR exon 19 deletion [+], PD-L1 20%) achieved SD (−28%) with a PFS of 6.4 months. After progression, he crossed over to cohort 2 and remained in PR for more than 1 year at the data cutoff date. These findings suggest that monotherapy may be insufficient for patients with de novo MET aberrations, underscoring the potential benefits of early dual-target therapy and reinforcing its therapeutic value in this specific patient population.
This prospective trial evaluated the potential efficacy of dual-targeted combination therapy as a first-line treatment for this patient population using precise selection criteria. As well-established, FISH is the gold standard for detecting MET amplification, and NGS can also be used. However, the threshold for NGS testing to define MET amplification is not uniform. The present study adopted the criterion used in the TATTON trial, which focused on the post-EGFR TKI resistance setting and defined MET amplification positivity as a tissue NGS MET gene copy number (GCN) ≥ 5. MET overexpression was primarily determined based on MET IHC testing using the Clinical Score criteria. However, the threshold for defining MET overexpression remains controversial. Previous studies of post-EGFR TKI resistance enrolled patients with MET IHC tumor cells ≥50% 2+ or 3+ in the INSIGHT study and ≥50% 3+ in the TATTON study, while the SAVANNAH study enrolled patients with MET IHC tumor cells ≥90% 3+ (Supplementary Table 1). There is no consensus on the definition of MET overexpression in the first-line setting due to limited supporting data. In our study, the definition of MET overexpression was based on our previous research findings27,28. MET overexpression was initially defined as over MET IHC 50% 3+, which revealed a significant difference in ORRs to first-line EGFR TKI and no significant difference in PFS between MET overexpression-positive and -negative groups. These findings highlight the value of precise patient selection and treatment strategies to improve outcomes in advanced NSCLC patients with EGFR mutations and de novo MET amplification and/or overexpression, signifying a potential benefit for this NSCLC subtype. In summary, the establishment of standardized MET testing criteria, coupled with refined biomarker strategies, will be critical for improving patient selection and ensuring the reproducibility and clinical applicability of such combination regimens in subsequent studies.
Osimertinib combined with savolitinib presented an acceptable safety and tolerability profile in this patient population, with safety findings consistent with the known profiles of individual therapies and previous study reported29. In this study, the combination therapy cohort exhibited a 57.1% incidence of grade 3 or higher TRAEs. Among them, most patients had grade 3 TRAEs, and no grade 5 AEs occurred in either of the cohorts. These TRAEs were effectively managed by dose reduction or treatment interruption. Only one patient in this study developed interstitial lung disease (grade 2) in the dual-targeted therapy cohort, leading to permanent discontinuation of both osimertinib and savolitinib.
The significance of this trial lies in two main aspects. First, it employs precise patient selection based on biomarkers for enrollment in the EGFR-mutant population. Second, it discloses the results of dual-target therapy in the MET-aberrant population. The primary limitations of this phase 2 study stem from its modest sample size and the absence of hypothesis testing. Although randomization was conducted, the baseline characteristics were imbalanced in some variables due to the limited number of patients. The prospective, randomized, phase 3 SANOVO study (NCT05009836) is currently in progress to confirm these results. Besides, the tumor response was not assessed by an independent review committee. Comprehensive data from all three MET assays were unavailable for some patients, and collecting these data could enhance our understanding of how MET aberrations influence treatment outcomes. Notably, most patients in this study had high MET IHC expression as a biomarker rather than MET amplification, making this trial predominantly focused on protein expression as a marker for primary resistance. Therefore, it is recommended that a formal assessment of MET amplification should be conducted in a separate trial specifically designed for this purpose.
In conclusion, this study indicated that osimertinib plus savolitinib as first-line treatment showed promising antitumor activity in newly diagnosed patients with EGFR-mutant advanced NSCLC with de novo MET amplification and/or overexpression. Longer-term follow-up is needed to evaluate the effects on survival-related endpoints. These results highlight the potential of this combination therapy as a viable first-line option and underscore the importance of precise treatment strategies for patients with EGFR mutations and MET aberrations.
Methods
Study design and patients
This phase 2, open-label, non-comparative, randomized, two-arm, multicenter, interventional study (ClinicalTrials.gov registration: NCT05163249), designated the CTONG 2008 (FLOWERS) study30, was conducted in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki, the Good Clinical Practice guidelines outlined by the International Council for Harmonisation, and all applicable regulatory requirements. The study protocol and amendments were approved by the independent ethics committees or institutional review boards at each participating center (Supplementary Table 6). All patients provided written informed consent. The authors confirm the accuracy and completeness of the data and adherence to the study protocol, which is fully accessible in Supplementary Note 1.
Patients aged 18 years or older with de novo MET amplifications and/or overexpression, EGFR-mutant, histologically or cytologically confirmed locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC who had not received any systemic anti-cancer therapy were enrolled. All patients had measurable disease based on computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in accordance with the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) 1.1 guidelines and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) or World Health Organization performance status of 0–1. Adequate liver function was required during screening. MET overexpression was defined as an IHC score of 3+ in at least 75% of tumor cells, based on our previous research. MET amplification was assessed by FISH with a MET GCN of ≥5, or MET/centromere-enriched protein 7 (CEP7) ratio of ≥2, or by NGS of tumor tissue, with ≥20% of tumor cells sequenced at a depth of ≥200× showing a copy number of ≥531,32. The complete eligibility criteria are listed in the Supplementary Note 1. Sex was recorded based on self-report.
Randomisation and masking
Patients were stratified according to the smoking status (yes, no), and EGFR mutation status (19 exon, 21 exon, other mutations) and randomly assigned (1:1) centrally using a computer-generated sequence with a minimization of dynamic randomization method developed by Guangdong Clinical Trial Association to receive either osimertinib monotherapy (cohort 1, 80 mg orally once daily) or combination therapy (cohort 2, osimertinib 80 mg orally once daily and savolitinib 300 mg orally twice daily). The enrollment of patients and assignment to trial cohorts were conducted by the investigators. There was no masking in this open-label study.
Procedures
Patients in cohort 1 who had disease progression with confirmed MET amplification and/or overexpression were allowed to crossover to cohort 2. In cohort 2, if one drug was discontinued due to AEs, the other drug was continued as a monotherapy.
Baseline ctDNA was analyzed using the Onco Sonar liquid biopsy test (Genetron Health Co., Ltd, China). Prior to the study treatment, 10 mL of blood samples were collected into Streck Cell-Free DNA Tubes. cfDNA was extracted using the MagMAX Cell-Free DNA Isolation Kit (Life Technologies) on the Kingfisher automated platform, and then quantified with a Qubit 2.0 Fluorometer (dsDNA HS assay, Life Technologies).
ctDNA analysis was performed on plasma ctDNA using the Onco Sonar liquid biopsy assay (Genetron Health Co., Ltd, China, catalog number RSN123), a hybrid capture–based NGS panel covering 172 cancer-related genes. NGS libraries were prepared with UMI barcodes to minimize the occurrence of sequencing artifacts. Then, the sequencing process was performed on the Genetron S2000 platform. The minimum depth across all targeted genes exceeded 20,000×, with depth exceeding 30,000× achieved for known hotspot regions.
EGFR exon 19 deletions were further filtered if detected at a variant allele frequency (VAF) of ≥0.5%, supported by a minimum of two independent cfDNA fragments. The assessment of MET amplification was conducted through a read-depth analysis, which was then compared to a panel of normal plasma controls. Amplification was defined as a depth ratio ≥1.15 and a z-score ≥3. In order to systematically characterize the genomic co-mutation landscape, all detected variants were evaluated across the 172-gene panel to identify additional genomic alterations. Finally, co-occurring mutations were summarized at the gene level to determine the prevalence of alterations within the patient cohort. The top three co-mutated genes detected in all these patients were further described in the results section.
Outcomes
The primary endpoint was the confirmed ORR assessed by the investigators. Key secondary endpoints included PFS, DoR, DCR, OS, and safety. Definitions for secondary endpoints are provided in the statistical analysis plan (SAP). Subgroup analyses were conducted across various patient populations based on baseline demographic and clinical characteristics.
Safety was assessed from the time of informed consent to 30 days post-final dose. AEs were graded according to the National Cancer Institute’s Common Terminology Criteria for AEs, version 5.0. TRAEs were determined by investigators. Baseline tumor assessments included CT or MRI scans of the chest and abdomen, covering the liver and adrenal glands. Tumor assessments were performed at week 4 (±7 days) and then every 8 weeks from treatment initiation until objective disease progression per RECIST 1.1 criteria.
Statistical analysis
No hypothesis testing was planned for this study, as all analyses were primarily descriptive. All analyses will be conducted based on the full analysis set (all randomized patients) unless specified otherwise. Based on expected ORRs of 44% for osimertinib monotherapy and 65% for the combination therapy, 22 subjects in each cohort, assuming a 10% dropout rate, will yield the specified precision using Clopper-Pearson’s exact method. Two analyses were planned: The first analysis focused on the primary endpoint of ORR, which was completed after all patients had two efficacy assessments (anticipated 12 weeks post-enrollment of the last patient). The second analysis focused on PFS, with a cutoff of approximately 40-month post-enrollment of the last patient based on a target PFS data maturity of 80%. Detailed analysis plans are described in the SAP.
Baseline demographics and clinical characteristics were summarized by treatment cohort. All variables were analyzed using descriptive statistical methods. Continuous variables were summarized by the number of observations, mean, standard deviation, median, minimum, and maximum values. Categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages for each category. The ORR, DCR, and their 95% CIs were descriptively summarized by cohort with percentages and 95% CIs estimated using the Clopper-Pearson method. The Kaplan-Meier method was used to estimate the median PFS. The number of patients, number of events, median and quartile PFS, PFS rates, and their 95% CIs at predefined landmarks were reported by cohort. AEs were summarized by the MedDRA system organ class and the preferred term. Statistical analysis of clinical data were performed using SAS version 9.4.

Peer review information

Data availability
The deidentified patient data are not publicly available due to restrictions imposed by the institutional review board. Reasonable requests will be reviewed by the Guangdong Provincial People’s Hospital. Access is restricted to qualified researchers for non-commercial academic use and will be shared in a deidentified format for 10 years after publication. Individual patient-level raw data containing identifiable patient information cannot be shared. Source data are provided with this paper. The ctDNA data generated in this study have been deposited in the Genome Sequence Archive, an approved public repository, under accession code HRA014210 and are publicly available. The remaining data are available within the Article, Supplementary Information or Source Data file. Source data are provided with this paper.
